content:
The body overseeing US President Donald Trump's plan to end the war in Gaza has accused both Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments, warning that the ceasefire is in danger of collapse and that more than two million Palestinians face another winter in tents and rubble. The 12-page report, seen by [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/trumps-board-peace-faults-israel-hamas-failure-end-gaza-war-2026-11-18/), is the Board of Peace's second to the United Nations Security Council since the US-backed ceasefire took effect 13 months ago, and it offers a sobering assessment of how little of the wider plan has actually been delivered.

"The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process," the report said, warning that "a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely." The board, which Trump established and chairs, is expected to present its findings to the Security Council in New York at the end of November.

The ceasefire itself has halted the major fighting, but almost everything that was supposed to follow it has stalled. Under the plan, Hamas was to disarm, Israeli troops were to withdraw and reconstruction was to begin. None of that has happened in any meaningful way. In July, Hamas agreed to a Board of Peace roadmap under which it would surrender its weapons and hand governance of Gaza to a civilian transitional authority. Israel rejected the roadmap, saying it will not withdraw until Hamas is dismantled — a position Defence Minister Israel Katz repeated on Wednesday, telling reporters that Israel would not pull out of Gaza until Hamas was dismantled and the territory demilitarised.

The report does not spare either side. It notes that Israel has carried out near-daily strikes on Gaza, and that Hamas fighters have continued attacks on Israeli troops. "Every day that Israel continues strikes against Hamas targets, it delays putting Hamas' agreement to the roadmap to the test," the report said. "Meanwhile, Hamas militant activity continues, the commitment to cease all military activities has not been met in full by the parties, and the population faces another winter in tents and rubble."

The warning came on the same day Israel's military said it had begun a concentrated operation in three areas of central Gaza, west of the so-called yellow line — the first such operation since the ceasefire took effect. That timing underlines the report's central point: the truce exists on paper, but the shooting has never fully stopped. More than 1,600 Palestinians, including many civilians, and five Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire was struck in October 2025, according to Reuters, while Gaza's health authorities put the Palestinian toll since the ceasefire at as many as 1,650.

Much of the report is devoted to the machinery that was supposed to replace the war and has not been built. It criticised Israel's government for what it called an "absence of decisions" on arrangements to train and deploy a civilian Palestinian police force to replace Hamas as Gaza's law enforcement authority, saying the delay was impeding the full implementation of the plan. It also said restrictions imposed by Israel on supplies and equipment, alongside funding shortfalls, had hindered the ability of Gazans to prepare for and respond to seasonal flooding. Heavy rain inundated displacement camps across Gaza last week, and more rain is expected later this month.

Hamas, for its part, was criticised for collecting taxes on goods entering Gaza, a practice the report said was affecting the availability of basic commodities. The result, the report suggests, is a population squeezed from both directions: aid and supplies constrained on entry, and prices pushed up once goods are inside.

The human picture behind those findings is stark. Gaza's population of more than two million Palestinians now lives confined to around a third of the coastal territory, mostly in makeshift tents and damaged buildings, under the control of Hamas fighters. Israel occupies the other two-thirds of Gaza, which has been largely razed and depopulated. The war began with the Hamas-led attacks of October 2023, in which around 1,200 people were killed in Israel; the Israeli assault on Gaza since then has killed 74,000 Palestinians, according to Reuters.

The report also exposes the political fragility around the plan. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing coalition remains in power in Israel in a caretaker capacity despite losing its majority in an inconclusive election last month, limiting its ability — or willingness — to take the decisions the Board of Peace is demanding. And while Trump's plan received strong international backing, the board itself has been met with scepticism from many of Washington's Western allies, who have questioned both its structure and its authority.

The board's first report was delivered in May by its director-general, Nickolay Mladenov, the former UN Middle East envoy. This second report is notably blunter, and its timing matters: it lands just as Trump prepares to host the leaders of China and Russia in Shenzhen, a summit that will test whether his personal diplomacy can still deliver results on the world stage, as [Global Wire reported](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/xi-trump-putin-summit-shenzhen-november-19). The Gaza file will now go before the Security Council at the end of the month, with the board's own verdict hanging over it — that the agreement is drifting, the population is paying the price, and a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot last.

Whether the report changes anything depends on the two parties it faults. Israel would have to accept the roadmap it rejected and approve the civilian police force it has not decided on; Hamas would have to stop its attacks and its taxation of incoming goods. Neither has shown any sign of doing so, and the region around Gaza remains volatile — as the wider escalation across the Gulf this week has shown, with US forces striking Iranian targets and Tehran retaliating, as [Global Wire reported](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/us-destroys-five-iranian-tankers-iran-retaliates-jordan-november-2026). For the people of Gaza, the report's warning is less a prediction than a description of the winter already under way.
summary: Donald Trump's Board of Peace has accused both Israel and Hamas of failing to meet their commitments under the Gaza ceasefire, warning in a 12-page report to the UN Security Council that the truce risks collapse and that more than two million Palestinians face another winter in tents and rubble.
title: Trump's Board of Peace faults Israel and Hamas as Gaza ceasefire risks collapse
